flawed_step: After showing that edge-transitivity (with no isolated vertices) gives at most two vertex orbits A and B, and that when A ≠ B the graph is bipartite with parts A and B and |A| = |B|, the proof needs an automorphism that swaps A and B. Nothing in the hypotheses provides one: regularity only matches degrees, and edge-transitivity acts on unordered edges, so it does not force any edge to be reversed.
counterexample: The Folkman graph (20 vertices, 4-regular) is edge-transitive but not vertex-transitive, i.e. semisymmetric. The Gray graph (54 vertices, cubic) is another example.
assessment_summary: Edge-transitivity with no isolated vertices gives at most two vertex orbits. If there are two, the graph is bipartite with equal-sized parts, but no hypothesis gives an automorphism swapping the parts. Semisymmetric graphs such as the Folkman graph are regular and edge-transitive but not vertex-transitive, so the statement is false.
